notes.meaning: David cries out for God to rescue him and clear his name by His mighty power. People from the town of Ziph had betrayed where he was hiding from King Saul. David has no one else to turn to, so he trusts God's character and strength to plead his cause.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Latin teaching reads David here as a figure of Christ and His church, where asking God to judge means separating the saved from the wicked rather than condemning them.

notes.meaning: David begs God to hear his words and pay attention to his distress. He speaks his prayer out loud to unload his fears before the Lord. He trusts that whenever God hears the honest cries of His servants, He will take action to help them.

Ruthless men are hunting David down to take his life. Even though the Ziphites belonged to David's own tribe of Judah, they acted like godless strangers because they treated him with cruel treachery. People who do not keep God before their eyes have no fear to stop them from doing evil.

David pauses in his trouble to declare that God is his true helper and the sustainer of his life. Even when God works through a few faithful human friends, the Lord is the real source of strength standing with them. Because the Almighty defends him, David knows his enemies cannot ultimately win.

David trusts that the harm his enemies planned for him will bounce back onto their own heads. He asks God to destroy their wicked plots because God made a faithful promise to protect him. Rather than taking personal revenge, David leaves the punishment entirely in God's hands.

David promises to bring a freewill offering to God with a cheerful and grateful heart. He is ready to praise the name of the Lord because God's character is loving and good. True worship comes from a willing spirit that thanks God for His rescue, not from forced duty.

differ.view: David meant both an inward willing heart and the outward animal sacrifices commanded by the Law of Moses.
David was not speaking of physical animal sacrifices under the Law, but of spiritual offerings of praise and thanksgiving from his lips.

notes.meaning: David speaks with complete faith, treating his future rescue as though it has already happened. God had spared him before and would safely deliver him from all his current dangers. He can look his retreating foes in the face without fear because God's justice has prevailed.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read this verse as personal gloating and a vengeful desire to see enemies suffer.
